LESSON OBJECTIVE
Identify randomized experiments, treatments, controls, response variables and valid causal conclusions.
CORE IDEA
An experiment actively assigns a treatment and measures its effect on an outcome. An observational study records what happens without assigning treatments.
KEY DEFINITIONS

Treatment: assigned condition. Response: measured outcome. Control group: comparison condition. Random assignment: chance-based allocation to treatments. Confounder: another factor affecting the outcome. Blinding: hiding treatment identity to reduce bias.
CORE RULE

A well-designed randomized experiment can support causal inference for the studied participants. Random sampling supports generalization; random assignment supports fair causal comparison. Neither guarantees perfect results.
HOW IT WORKS

Identify who participates, which factor is deliberately changed, the response being measured, the control condition, and whether assignment is random. Check blinding, replication, attrition and potential confounders.
WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — EXPERIMENT
Researchers randomly assign students to tutoring or standard instruction, then compare test scores. The assigned tutoring is the treatment; test score is the response.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — OBSERVATIONAL CONTRAST
Researchers record which students independently choose tutoring. Because tutoring was not assigned, the comparison is observational and prior motivation may confound results.
WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — DIFFERENCE IN RATES
In two groups of 100, 70 treated participants improve versus 50 controls. Rates are 0.70 and 0.50; observed difference is 0.20, or 20 percentage points.
WORKED EXAMPLE 4 — RANDOM ASSIGNMENT
A trial assigns 120 people equally to three groups using random allocation. Each group receives 40 participants; chance helps balance other characteristics across groups.
WORKED EXAMPLE 5 — GENERALIZATION
Randomly assigned volunteers from one school may support a causal comparison among those volunteers, but the convenience sample may not represent all schools.
WORKED EXAMPLE 6 — BIAS
If 40% of treated participants leave a study but only 10% of controls leave, differential attrition threatens the validity of the final comparison.
COMMON MISTAKES
Do not confuse random assignment with random sampling. A control group need not receive nothing; it may receive standard care or placebo. An observed difference is not automatically free from bias.
EXAM STRATEGY

Look for verbs such as assigned, allocated and randomized. Find the measured outcome and comparison group. Compute rate differences using the same units and distinguish percentage points from percent change.
QUICK CHECK
Q1: Assigning fertilizer to plots is an experiment. Q2: 30/60−18/60=0.20. Q3: Random assignment supports causal comparisons; random sampling supports generalization.
LESSON RECAP
Experiments assign treatments and compare outcomes. Random assignment, controls, blinding and replication strengthen evidence; representative sampling is a separate question.
